Posted May 7, 2003
(MarijuanaNews note: Yesterday, the Canadian Supreme Court finally heard the oral arguments in the challenges to all aspects of cannabis prohibition in Canada that it was supposed to hear in December.
See
 Canadian Supreme Court Punts On Cannabis Cases Until Spring. The Games Governments Play Prove The Need for International Debate on Cannabis Prohibition. Special to MarijuanaNews

There are really three different cases, involving three different defendants. The Caine case is the simplest, and the one that we have the best chance of winning. It involves a 1993 arrest for possession of a tiny roach the butt of a cannabis joint. Caine is being represented by my good friend John Conroy, QC.
See
 Canadian Prime Minister Commits To Decriminalization Soon Just 23 Years After He First Said He Was In Favor. It Was A Good Idea Then, But John Conroy Thinks It May Be Dangerous Now.

I talked with John yesterday evening and he was generally pleased with the way things went, but Supreme Court Justices make great poker players. [Don't tell Bill Bennett.]

The Clay case involves the sale of seeds and seedlings, and the Malmo-Levine case involves retail sales.

The implications of each case goes a bit further than just the details of the charges. For example, the Caine case could end with a ruling that just having small amounts for personal use cannot be a crime, or it could also allow for cultivation for personal use. The Clay case could include cultivation for sale. And the M-L case could include any sales.

Obviously, there is more reason for optimism for the Caine case than the others, because the Court is more likely to defer to Parliament on sales. Nonetheless, it is entirely possible that the Court will declare all of the laws unconstitutional, because virtually all of the findings of fact in the lower courts have been in our favor.
See
Extraordinary Editorial in Winnipeg Free Press Outlines " Findings of Fact " In Possession Case to Be Heard by Canadian Supreme Court.

It is hoped that the Court will rule by the end of the year, but it could be well into 2004 before they rule. In the meantime, the Court's involvement casts a long shadow over the pending decriminalization bill that is supposed to be introduced in the Parliament before the June recess, although some think that they will not act on it.

In fact, there is another reason that they may wait on the Court. If the Court rules that any of the laws violate the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, then voiding those laws does not violate the UN treaties, all of which are " subject to " the constitutions of the signatories. That could have major international implications. No one else seems to have noticed this very important point.
See
Swiss Government Says Going Dutch Does NOT Violate Treaties. Implications for Other Countries, Especially Canada and UK. Plus Full Text of UN Nark Press Release.

In any case, the narks are in a dilemma. If they introduce a phony decriminalization bill that would have escalating fines and allow for jailing either repeat offenders or people who cannot pay their fines, then the Court is even more likely to throw out the possession laws than they would be if there is a bill that is toothless. The Court might have more hearings if there is such a change, but the challenges are to the fundamental questions, so they might not.

Moreover, if the government's decriminalization is real but includes harsher penalties for growing, as DEAland has been urging, then that increases the likelihood of the Court deciding that those laws are also unreasonable.

What ever is a nark to do?! Poor dears. Well, they could just read the DEAland papers, if ignorance is bliss. Although there was extensive coverage in Canada, I could not find anything about the Court hearings, and almost nothing about the pending decrim bill in any of DEAland's major prohibitionist propaganda outlets web sites, i.e., The New York Times, Washington Post, etc.

However, there was one priceless example of the sort of pseudojournalism that is typical of the media's handling of the cannabis issue on the Yahoo-Reuters news site.
See
 We Have Reality Entertainment, So What About Some Reality News? Public Distrust And The Reality/Media Credibility Gap.

Yahoo News has a variety of categories for articles, Top Stories, Business, World, etc., and a search engine that I use everyday. Today, a search under marijuana brought nothing about the Canadian Court. Zilch. However, I sometimes check their Oddly Enough novelty news index page for a laugh, and guess what. There it was under the headline, Dude, Is This the High Court?
See
 Dude, You're Getting A Journalism Lesson. The Media Won't Report How Many Cannabis Arrests There Are In DEAland, or New York City, But This Celebrity Arrest Is Even Reported In The Washington Post.
and
 How the Success of NORML's New York Ad Campaign Demonstrates The Failure of the Mass Media to Serve Democracy.
Does Reporting on Marijuana Lower The Media's IQ (Integrity Quotient)?
and
 At Least the Libertarians Are Noting the Record Marijuana Arrests and Offer an Interesting Perspective. The Media Continue to be the Watchdog that Never Barks.
and
 Great Critiques Of Media Bias In Reporting On Marijuana From News Watch Ezine -- Two Articles

That's right. A constitutional challenge to cannabis prohibition next door at the Supreme Court level, is a novelty item. I have written in the past about how this sort of reporting with puns and sneers in the headlines help condition readers not to take the subject seriously. It's only marijuana, ha ha. Move along there is nothing here for you to think about. I call it the giggle factor. Dan Gardner of the Ottawa Citizen prefers snicker. It is just one more reason why I say that bad journalism is the best two-word explanation for the war on cannabis and why we have to take back the media.)
See
 Author of Ottawa Citizen Series on Prohibition Blames The Media for the Drug War. Great Journalism Is The Antidote.
and
Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th Commandments.

Dude, Is This the High Court?
 May 7, 2003
From The Oddly Enough section of Reuters on Yahoo!
By Randall Palmer
(MarijuanaNews note: Reporters don't usually write the headlines and have no control over the placement of their articles. Of course, it is also impossible to know how much it has been edited. I have had reporters call me after an article has been printed under their name and whisper, That's not the way I wrote it.)

OTTAWA (Reuters) - There is now another reason to call it Canada's high court.

" I took a couple hits off some bubble hash and a little bit of cannabis, " David Malmo-Levine told reporters after delivering a 40-minute monologue to the nine justices.

" I was happy, hungry and relaxed, but I was not impaired. "

But his arguments seem to have fallen a little flat with the justices, who will not rule for a number of months.
(MarijuanaNews note: No substance, just color.)

After having mercilessly grilled a lawyer arguing a companion case, they declined to question Malmo-Levine despite his pleas to " hammer away " at him.

His arguments were nothing if not innovative, however.
(MarijuanaNews note: Now we have an opinion.)

He argued that just as the court had created a prohibition against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, he should receive similar constitutional protection on the basis of " substance orientation " and " vocation orientation. "
(MarijuanaNews note: In the Canadian context, this is a reasonable argument.)

" A natural preference or taste for herbs is a substance orientation, " said the 31-year-old university dropout, sporting a black shirt, jacket, pants and boots, white tie, and multicolored " hankie, " all made from hemp.

" Why should not cannabis cafe operators receive vocation orientation protection? "

He was charged in 1996 with possession of marijuana for the purposes of trafficking, when police raided a " Harm Reduction Club " in Vancouver which provided pot to its 1,800 members and which he helped run.

Appealing to the court to strike down the law, he said: " For the vast section of people all over the world who have an innate feeling deep down inside they should have a right to self-medicate and control their own minds, you'll be heroes. "

Ironically, the federal government defended the law before the Supreme Court even though it plans to decriminalize the possession of small amounts of marijuana.

The chief federal lawyer arguing the case, David Frankel, told Reuters that even under the proposed changes to the law, the government would keep criminal penalties for possession of larger amounts of pot and for trafficking in the substance.

Ottawa's plans have drawn warnings from the Bush administration of a possible crackdown at the U.S. border.

In the Supreme Court chamber, Malmo-Levine's supporters, with a mixture of pony-tails and bushy beards, flannel shirts and T-shirts emblazoned with the marijuana plant, stood out from the well-heeled legal crowd.
(MarijuanaNews note: Many people would prefer that colorful characters like David stay in the closet, while only people who look like me, but maybe with a little more hair, be allowed to appear in court. However, where were they when David was getting beaten by the Vancouver police? Waiting until it was safe to come out of their own closets. The gay rights movement began in New York when drag queens rioted after the police raided the Stonewall bar. David is right in arguing that people like him should be free to be like him. That is what freedom is all about.)

Lawyer Paul Burstein, appearing ahead of Malmo-Levine, argued that the drug is harmless to 19 out of 20 users, but Justice Ian Binnie said 30,000 to 50,000 heavy users in Canada were still at risk of mental deterioration and other problems.
See
 American Journal Of Epidemiology Report That Long-Term Use Of Marijuana
Does Not Lead To A Decline In Mental Function Got Minimal Coverage,
Perhaps Because Scores Actually Fell More Among Non-Users Than Among Heavy Users!

Justice Charles Gonthier asked if the balancing of how harmful marijuana is was not a political question.

Burstein responded that " there is an insufficient amount of harm to warrant the very heavy hammer of the criminal law, " and therefore courts should in fact interfere.
